infrastructure.secret_management: supabase edge function secrets + vite env

findings.title: School registration fails for every real user (RLS blocks the RETURNING clause)
findings.description: registerOrder() calls .insert({...}).select().single() on schools. supabase-js turns .select() into the PostgREST header Prefer: return=representation, which makes Postgres run INSERT ... RETURNING. RETURNING requires the SELECT policy to pass. The only SELECT policy on schools is organizer-only, so anon fails with 42501. Every school that submits the registration form gets 'Could not register school.'
findings.exploit_scenario: Not an attack. A school fills in the registration form and submits. The INSERT itself is permitted, but the RETURNING clause is denied by RLS, so supabase-js surfaces an error and the flow aborts. The school cannot register at all. A partial school row may be left behind by the permitted INSERT.
findings.impact: Total loss of the store's primary function. No school can order a kit. Registration opens 31 August.
findings.recommendation: Stop reading the row back. Generate the school id client-side with crypto.randomUUID() and insert without .select(). Better: move the whole registration into an Edge Function using the service role, which also fixes finding 2.
findings.verification: curl against live PostgREST: plain INSERT returns HTTP 201; identical INSERT with Prefer: return=representation returns HTTP 401 code 42501.
findings.notes: Pre-existing, inherited from the Next.js MVP which used the same anon client with .select(). The prior policy auth.role()='authenticated' was also false for anon, so the role migration did not introduce this. It was previously reported as verified-working on the strength of a raw SQL INSERT, which has no RETURNING clause and therefore did not exercise the same code path.

findings.title: Anonymous users can forge orders as paid and dispatched
findings.description: The INSERT policies on orders and schools are with_check (true). Any holder of the publishable key, which ships in the JavaScript of every page, can POST directly to /rest/v1/orders and set every column freely, including status, total_amount, kit_unit_price, paid_at and dispatched_at. The server-side price snapshot inside registerOrder is not a security control because the attacker never runs the app.
findings.exploit_scenario: 1. Read the publishable key from the page source. 2. POST a schools row with an attacker-chosen UUID so the id is known without needing read access. 3. POST an orders row referencing it with team_count 50, total_amount 1, status dispatched and a backdated paid_at. 4. The order appears in the organizer console as a legitimate dispatched order and is readable through the public get_order_status RPC.
findings.impact: Fraudulent kit claims. 50 primary kits is about NGN 2.35m of hardware shown as paid and dispatched with NGN 1 recorded. Confirmed revenue statistics are corrupted, and unlimited junk orders can be injected.
findings.recommendation: Revoke anon INSERT on orders and schools. Move order creation into an Edge Function that uses the service role and sets status, prices and timestamps itself, accepting only school details, division and team count from the client.
findings.verification: Executed against the live project: schools INSERT HTTP 201, orders INSERT HTTP 201 with status=dispatched, then confirmed readable via rpc/get_order_status. Test rows deleted.

findings.title: Unauthenticated unlimited upload to the payment-proofs bucket
findings.description: The storage policy allows INSERT to payment-proofs from anyone with only bucket_id checked. The bucket has file_size_limit null and allowed_mime_types null, so any file of any type and any size can be written to any path, with no order needing to exist.
findings.exploit_scenario: A script uploads arbitrary files to arbitrary paths in a loop. No order, no reference and no account are required. Storage grows without bound.
findings.impact: Unbounded storage cost on your Supabase bill, arbitrary third-party content parked in your bucket, and possible quota exhaustion that would break genuine proof uploads during the payment window.
findings.recommendation: Set file_size_limit to about 5MB and allowed_mime_types to image/jpeg, image/png and application/pdf on the bucket. Narrow the policy so the path prefix must match an existing order reference.
findings.verification: Uploaded text/html to payment-proofs/NOT-AN-ORDER/cso-audit.html as anon: HTTP 200, with no corresponding order. Anon DELETE correctly refused (HTTP 400), so the test object needs manual removal.

findings.title: Order reference, used as a bearer credential, is generated with Math.random()
findings.description: generateOrderReference() builds the reference from Math.random(). That reference is the sole credential authenticating both get_order_status and submit_payment_proof. V8 implements Math.random() as xorshift128+, which is not cryptographically secure and whose internal state can be recovered from observed outputs.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers several orders and collects the references. Because the underlying generator is a recoverable PRNG rather than a CSPRNG, sampled outputs narrow the state and make other tenants' references predictable rather than requiring a full 32^6 search. A predicted reference exposes order details and permits a forged proof submission via finding 6.
findings.impact: Order detail disclosure and forged proof-of-payment attachment against other schools' orders.
findings.recommendation: Use crypto.getRandomValues() to index the alphabet. One-line change. Add a retry loop on unique-violation, since the column is UNIQUE and there is currently no collision handling.

findings.title: Recovery email endpoint has no rate limit
findings.description: send-order-confirmation enforces a 60 second cooldown through orders.confirmation_sent_at, but recover-order-references has no equivalent throttle. It is verify_jwt=false with Access-Control-Allow-Origin *, so any page or script can call it repeatedly.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who knows a school's contact address posts to the endpoint in a loop, delivering an email each time. The victim's inbox is flooded and the project's Resend sending quota and reputation are consumed.
findings.impact: Inbox flooding of a real school, exhausted email quota, and possible sender-reputation damage that causes genuine confirmations to be filtered.
findings.recommendation: Record a last-sent timestamp per address and apply the same 60 second cooldown used by the confirmation function. Consider a per-IP limit as well.
findings.verification: Read the deployed source; no cooldown, counter or timestamp check exists on any path.

findings.title: submit_payment_proof writes an unvalidated, caller-supplied storage path
findings.description: The security-definer RPC accepts proof_path as a free-form string and writes it to proof_of_payment_url with no check that the path exists, sits under that order's prefix, or was uploaded by the submitter. It is anon-callable and authenticated only by the order reference.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker uploads a forged receipt using finding 3, then calls submit_payment_proof with a known or predicted reference (finding 4) and their own path. The organizer opens the attacker's file believing it is the school's receipt and may confirm a payment that never arrived.
findings.impact: An organizer can be induced to mark an unpaid order as paid and dispatch a kit.
findings.recommendation: Validate inside the function that proof_path starts with the order reference followed by a slash, and that a matching storage object exists.
findings.verification: Read the function definition via pg_get_functiondef; the body performs a bare UPDATE with no validation of proof_path. Partial mitigation confirmed: status only moves registered to payment_pending and never downgrades an already-paid order.

findings.title: Registration performs two unlinked writes, orphaning school rows
findings.description: registerOrder inserts a school and then an order as two separate PostgREST calls with no transaction. If the second write fails, the school row persists. There is also no dedupe on contact_email, so a school ordering twice becomes two unrelated records.
findings.exploit_scenario: Not an attack. Given finding 1 the second step currently fails on every attempt, so each registration attempt leaves an orphaned school row behind and the table fills with unusable records.
findings.impact: Corrupted registration data and inflated school counts, which will misreport participation figures.
findings.recommendation: Perform both writes inside one Edge Function against the service role so they share a transaction, and upsert the school on contact_email.
findings.verification: Read src/lib/store.ts:120-155; two sequential awaits with no transactional wrapper and no cleanup on the failure path.

findings.title: team_count has no upper bound
findings.description: The only constraint is the database check team_count > 0. The client-side minimum of 1 is not a server control, and any integer up to 2147483647 is accepted.
findings.exploit_scenario: A caller submits team_count 2147483647, producing a total_amount near 1e14 naira. Combined with finding 2 this can be done at will and repeatedly.
findings.impact: Absurd orders in the organizer console and corrupted revenue aggregates, which are summed client-side without sanity limits.
findings.recommendation: Add a database check constraint such as team_count between 1 and 100, and mirror it in the Edge Function that will own order creation.
findings.verification: Read the table definition; the only constraint present is team_count > 0.
